title: K-th Element of Two Sorted Arrays
statement:
You are given two arrays `a` (length `m`) and `b` (length `n`), each sorted in non-decreasing order, and an integer `k`. Imagine merging both arrays into one sorted sequence of `m + n` values, **keeping duplicates**. Return the `k`-th smallest value of that merged sequence (1-indexed, so `k = 1` is the minimum).

The interviewer expects a solution that does not merge the arrays: it should run in `O(log(min(m, n)))` time by binary searching on how many elements are taken from the shorter array. (The input itself still has to be read in `O(m + n)`; the complexity below refers to the search.)
inputFormat:
The first line contains three integers `m`, `n` and `k`.
The second line contains `m` integers: the elements of `a` in non-decreasing order.
The third line contains `n` integers: the elements of `b` in non-decreasing order.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the `k`-th smallest element of the merged sequence.
constraints: Both arrays are sorted in non-decreasing order

examples.explanation: The merged sequence is `1 2 3 4 5 8 9`; its 4th element is 4.
The merged sequence is `5 5 5 5 7`. Duplicates count separately, so the 3rd smallest value is 5.
The merged sequence is `-3 10`; the 2nd element is 10.

hints: Merging takes O(m + n). Instead, ask: how many of the k smallest elements come from `a`? Call it `i`; then `k - i` come from `b`.
A split `i` is correct when `a[i-1] ≤ b[k-i]` and `b[k-i-1] ≤ a[i]` (treat out-of-range neighbours as -∞ / +∞). Binary search `i` over `[max(0, k-n), min(k, m)]`.
If `a[i-1] > b[k-i]` you took too many from `a`, so move left; otherwise move right. The answer is `max(a[i-1], b[k-i-1])`. Search on the shorter array.
